poems:
Somebody's fork still in somebody's tupperware,
back of the fridge,
a name written on tape.
1:01. The agenda says fifteen minutes. The agenda has said fifteen minutes since March.

The forklift beeps in reverse,
the same three notes,
all afternoon.
Everyone agrees. Nobody moves.

Things on the break room table:
half a sheet cake,
a spatula,
a card nobody has signed.
1:05. Somewhere a whole country has closed for two hours and is not sorry about it.
Bread still in your back teeth when they call on you.
A pallet jack parked crooked against the loading dock rail.

Digestion is a full-time job
and it has just taken the wheel.
The plan for the day, revised downward.
Post-lunch, adj.: the condition of having agreed at 12:40 to something you cannot now recall.
1:11. The warehouse radio switches to the station nobody chose and everybody accepts.
Grass clippings stuck in a wet stripe along the sidewalk.
1:13. Somebody's alarm goes off. Nobody admits it was theirs.
Overheard: I'm not saying we redo it. I'm saying we look at it fresh.
Quarter past. The line at the taco truck is finally short and the good ones are gone.
Coffee, second attempt.

A man in a hard hat asleep in his truck,
seat back, boots on the dash,
phone face down on his chest.
1:18. You have read the same paragraph four times and each time it was fine.
The mail comes. A catalog, a solicitation, and the one thing that matters, which is a bill.
Someone microwaves fish. War begins.
Stand up. Walk to the far bathroom, not the near one. Take the long way back. That is the whole strategy.
Two forklifts passing in an aisle, drivers not looking up.
In the ICU the shift change alters nothing about the room, only who is standing in it.
The riding mower finishes the long side and turns. The engine drops a note going uphill.
Nobody has said anything for four minutes.

SUB TOTAL 11.42
TAX 0.91
CASH 20.00
CHANGE 7.67
THANK YOU COME AGAIN
SERVER: DEE

If it's a weekday, the third hour of somebody's shift.
If it isn't, a mower somewhere, going.
The vending machine takes the dollar, thinks about it, returns the dollar. Twice.

Half the office insists it works better in the afternoon.
Half the office is asleep behind sunglasses in a parked car.
Bottom of the hour. Fourteen slides left, a warm room, and a voice going gently on.
A dog stretched flat across a doorway.
1:32. Somebody a long way east is turning off a lamp. Somebody west is four hours from waking.
The email will get answered today. That decision has now been made three times.
A hairnet, a walk-in door, a crate of romaine sweating on a steel table.

KEEP AREA CLEAR
DO NOT STACK ABOVE THIS LINE
MAX LOAD 2,000 LBS
1:36. Nothing happens. It takes a while.
The good chair by the window is taken by a man doing nothing in it.
Second lunch, quietly, from the desk drawer.

A crossing guard eats standing up beside a stop sign,
vest folded on the hood,
hours yet before anyone needs her.
1:40. The part of the day that gets no photographs.
A truck idles behind the grocery, ramp down, nobody on it.
The all-hands ends early and the relief in the room is audible and slightly embarrassing.
1:43. Two people are pretending to look at the same spreadsheet.
Somebody's yawn goes around the table like money.
Quarter to. Tonight's onions are already chopped, in a hotel pan, under plastic, waiting.

Afternoon inventory:
one pen that works,
one that doesn't,
a hair tie,
sixty cents,
a receipt from a place that closed.
Somebody says circle back and means never.
A dropped glove on the parking lot line, palm up, fingers curled.

In a parked car, seat reclined,
fifteen minutes that will not be entered anywhere.
Ten to two. Still plenty of afternoon left, unfortunately.
1:51. A woman in a warehouse aisle scans a barcode and the gun chirps yes.

A shutter comes down over a shop door for two hours.
Somewhere else a man eats standing at a sink.
The dishwasher starts its second load and the kitchen smells like hot plastic.
A fly, methodical, working the window.
People have started saying end of day about things that will not happen at end of day.
The paperwork gets a signature and a date and goes into a tray where it will sit until Thursday.
1:57. Three minutes left and one thing crossed off the list, which was writing the list.
The room agrees to keep going.

The mower comes to the fence line,
turns,
goes back across everything it just did.
